headline: Fast-Money Systematic Funds Stoked $2.3 Trillion Tech-Stock Rout
author: Natalia Kniazhevich

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- As investors rushed out of US technology stocks on Thursday, selling by trend-following systematic strategies amplified what quickly became a record plunge by market value in the Nasdaq 100 index.

The tech benchmark sank 6.4%, erasing $2.3 trillion in market value, the most ever in a single day. Concerns that a Democratic sweep could mean tighter regulation of the AI buildout, crimping growth for chipmakers and data-center suppliers at the heart of the equity market's bullish run, drove the move.

As those worries pushed major indexes below key technical levels, systematic funds were forced to cut exposure, speeding the decline, according to equity derivatives strategists at JPMorgan Chase & Co. Unlike traditional investors, these quantitative funds typically follow the direction of the stock market, responding to price movements and momentum signals rather than company fundamentals.

Commodity trading advisers, or CTAs, as well as other trend-following strategies likely deleveraged sharply, turning net short US equities, the JPMorgan strategists led by Bram Kaplan said in a note. The decline broke several key momentum signals across major US indexes during the morning session, triggering additional selling by CTAs.
Net selling in S&P 500 futures totaled about $11 billion during the first hour and a half of cash trading, according to JPMorgan data.

Selling pressure from systematic strategies may not be over. Volatility-targeting portfolios have an estimated $50 billion of equity exposure to sell over the next few days, as they cut target leverage to around the 30th percentile from the 67th, according to the JPMorgan team's model.

Separately, Barclays Equities Tactical Strategies models show that these funds could reduce equity exposure by about 30 percentage points, one of the largest one-day adjustments since the Covid-era market turmoil. The funds could sell roughly $135 billion in US equity futures over the next 24 to 48 hours, the models show.

The JPMorgan team said that leveraged exchange-traded funds also sharply reduced exposure for the second time in a week, with the latest selling once again concentrated in technology. The funds sold more than $60 billion of stocks into the close, with about 90% of this tied to technology-related products, including semiconductors, Nasdaq 100 and technology-sector ETFs, they said.

With leveraged ETFs having already cut exposure sharply, their potential rebalancing flows should be smaller going forward. Their implicit short-gamma exposure has declined to about $6.5 billion per 1% market move from roughly $7.5 billion, the strategists' estimates show.
"Investor dip-buying inflows may have offset some of this rebalancing need, as in past selloffs," Kaplan wrote.
